intro: Today you polish three things that make your English easy to understand: endings with two or three consonants (asked = 'askt', months, texts), pairs of words that differ in just one sound (live / leave, fan / van), and stress that moves inside a word family (PHO-to-graph → pho-TO-gra-phy). Warm-up: say 'I asked for six months' slowly, then fast.
teachingNotes: Final clusters (gugus konsonan = two or three consonant sounds together, no vowel between): build on a1-pron-word-stress (desk, lunch) and a2-pron-ed-weak-forms (-ed = t / d / id). Grammar endings stack consonants: ask + -ed = asked 'askt' (s + k + t; British 'aaskt', American 'askt'), help + -ed = helped 'helpt', month + -s = months 'manths', text + -s = texts 'teksts', crisp + -s = crisps 'krisps' (British crisps = American chips = keripik kentang), next 'nekst'. Node common error: asked said 'ask' or 'as'. Indonesian trap: Indonesian words almost never end in two consonants (only loanwords like pers, korps), and Indonesian even borrowed text as 'teks', dropping the final t. So learners drop sounds ('as' for asked, 'mon' for months, 'teks' for texts) or add a vowel ('as-ked', 'help-e'). Dropping changes the meaning: asked → ask (the past is lost), texts → text (the plural is lost).

Drill: slow, then fast. Build the ending piece by piece ('as' → 'ask' → 'askt'), then the word at normal speed, then in a sentence. Before a vowel, carry the last sound over (asked a question → 'ask-tə question', six months ago → 'manth-sə-GOU'); before a consonant, keep it small and quick with no added vowel. Be honest: in fast speech native speakers simplify the hardest clusters (months often 'mants' or 'mans', texts 'tekss'); sixths ('siksths') is hard even for natives: mention it only as a note, never drill or test it. What must survive is the final s (plural, he/she) and the final t/d (past).

Minimal pairs (explain the term: two words that differ in only one sound, like Indonesian pagi / bagi). Recap a0-sounds-indonesian in one line (ship / sheep, th, v) and go further: real sentences where the wrong sound changes the meaning. Short quick 'i' vs long 'ii' (held longer, lips spread like a smile): live / leave, fill / feel, sit / seat. Short 'u' vs long 'uu' (lips round): full / fool, pull / pool. f vs v: fan / van, ferry / very, safe / save; v = top teeth on the lower lip WITH a buzz in the throat; Indonesian usually says the letter v like f (visa, televisi). th vs s / t: think / sink, thank / tank, three / tree; tongue tip lightly between the teeth, air only. Node common errors: van said as 'fan'; live and leave said the same way. leave ends in v, so 'liif' sounds like leaf. pen / pan only if the learner asks. Spelling clues: ee / ea are usually the long 'ii'; oo can be long (fool, food) or short (good, book), so learn each word with its sound.

Stress shift in word families: build on b1-word-formation (in-for-MA-tion, em-ploy-EE) and a1-pron-word-stress. These endings pull the stress to the syllable just before them: -ic / -ical, -ian, -tion / -sion, -ity, -graphy: PHO-to-graph → pho-TO-gra-phy → pho-to-GRA-phic; PO-li-tics → po-LI-ti-cal → po-li-TI-cian; e-CON-o-my → e-co-NOM-ic (economy is NOT stressed on the first syllable); ED-u-cate → ed-u-CA-tion; AC-tive → ac-TI-vi-ty. Endings that don't move it: -er, -ment, -ful, -less, -ly (TEACH-er, em-PLOY-ment, HELP-ful). Exception to name: photographer follows photography (pho-TO-gra-pher). The vowels change too: the strong syllable is clear, the others often go to the lazy schwa ('FOU-tə-graaf' vs 'fə-TOG-rə-fi'; American 'FOU-tə-graf'). Indonesian trap: similar Indonesian words (fotografi, ekonomi, politik) are said with an even rhythm, so learners keep one stress for the whole family. For typed checks, ask 'first, second, third or fourth syllable' (answers are lowercased, so capitals can't be checked).

Limits: grammar A0–A2 plus b1-word-formation only (no passive, past perfect, relative clauses or second conditional). Respellings in quotes use everyday letters; CAPITALS = the strong syllable; ə only together with 'the short e of emas'. No bare IPA. Don't teach sentence rhythm or intonation (that's b1-pron-rhythm-intonation), secondary stress, or a full list of every suffix rule.

keyPoints.title: Say the whole ending: asked, months, texts
keyPoints.explanation: Grammar endings stack consonants at the end of a word: asked = 'askt' (s + k + t), months = 'manths', texts = 'teksts'. Indonesian words almost never end like this, so learners drop sounds ('as' for asked). But the ending is the meaning: no t = not past, no s = only one. Practise slowly ('as… ask… askt'), then fast, and carry the last sound over to a next word that starts with a vowel ('ask-tə question').

examples.en: Sari asked a question in the meeting.
We lived in Surabaya for six months.
examples.id: Kami tinggal di Surabaya selama enam bulan.

examples.en: I sent you two texts this morning.
examples.id: Aku mengirim dua pesan ke kamu tadi pagi.

id.title: Ucapkan akhirannya sampai habis: asked, months, texts
id.explanation: Akhiran tata bahasa menumpuk konsonan di akhir kata: asked = 'askt' (s + k + t), months = 'manths', texts = 'teksts'. Kata bahasa Indonesia hampir tidak pernah berakhir seperti ini, jadi pelajar sering menghilangkan bunyi ('as' untuk asked). Padahal akhiran itulah maknanya: tanpa t = bukan lampau, tanpa s = hanya satu. Latihan pelan-pelan dulu ('as… ask… askt'), lalu cepat, dan sambungkan bunyi terakhir ke kata berikutnya yang diawali vokal ('ask-tə question').

keyPoints.title: Minimal pairs: live / leave, full / fool, fan / van, think / sink
keyPoints.explanation: A minimal pair is two words that differ in only one sound. Short quick 'i' (live 'liv') vs long 'ii' with a smile (leave 'liiv'); short 'u' (full 'ful') vs long 'uu' with round lips (fool 'fuul'). v = top teeth on the lower lip WITH a buzz (van), f = air only (fan). th = tongue tip between the teeth (think), not s (sink) or t.

examples.en: I live in Depok, but I work in Jakarta.
examples.id: Aku tinggal di Depok, tapi kerja di Jakarta.

examples.en: We leave the office at five.
examples.id: Kami pulang dari kantor jam lima.

examples.en: Pak Hasan drives a white van.
examples.id: Pak Hasan menyetir mobil van putih.

id.title: Minimal pairs: live / leave, full / fool, fan / van, think / sink
id.explanation: Minimal pair adalah dua kata yang hanya beda satu bunyi. 'i' pendek dan cepat (live 'liv') vs 'ii' panjang sambil tersenyum (leave 'liiv'); 'u' pendek (full 'ful') vs 'uu' panjang dengan bibir bulat (fool 'fuul'). v = gigi atas menyentuh bibir bawah DAN tenggorokan bergetar (van), f = hanya udara (fan). th = ujung lidah di antara gigi (think), bukan s (sink) atau t.

keyPoints.title: The stress moves in a word family
keyPoints.explanation: Some endings pull the stress to the syllable just before them: -ic, -ical, -ian, -tion, -ity, -graphy. PHO-to-graph → pho-TO-gra-phy → pho-to-GRA-phic; PO-li-tics → po-LI-ti-cal → po-li-TI-cian; e-CON-o-my → e-co-NOM-ic. Endings like -er, -ment, -ful don't move it (TEACH-er, em-PLOY-ment), but photographer follows photography: pho-TO-gra-pher.

examples.en: He doesn't like talking about politics.

id.title: Tekanan berpindah dalam keluarga kata
id.explanation: Beberapa akhiran menarik tekanan ke suku kata tepat sebelum akhiran itu: -ic, -ical, -ian, -tion, -ity, -graphy. PHO-to-graph → pho-TO-gra-phy → pho-to-GRA-phic; PO-li-tics → po-LI-ti-cal → po-li-TI-cian; e-CON-o-my → e-co-NOM-ic. Akhiran seperti -er, -ment, -ful tidak memindahkannya (TEACH-er, em-PLOY-ment), tapi photographer mengikuti photography: pho-TO-gra-pher.

guidedPractice.prompt: Dimas says: 'Turn left at the nex corner.' Which word did he mean? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: The word ends in three consonant sounds: k, s, t ('nekst').

guidedPractice.prompt: How many beats (syllables) does 'jumped' have? Write the number.
guidedPractice.hint: jump ends in p, a sound with no buzz, so -ed is just a small t: 'jampt'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which word has the long 'ii' sound: sit or seat? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: ea is usually the long 'ii': hold it longer and smile.

guidedPractice.prompt: For which sound do your top teeth touch your lower lip AND your throat buzzes: f or v? Write the letter.
guidedPractice.hint: Hand on your throat: say ffff, then vvvv. Which one shakes?

guidedPractice.prompt: Which part of 'photography' is stressed: pho, to, gra or phy? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: -graphy pulls the stress to the syllable just before it.

independentPractice.prompt: Rina writes how she said a sentence: 'I finish the report yesterday.' Write the verb the way it should be.
independentPractice.hint: It's the past: finish + -ed. sh has no buzz, so -ed is a small t: 'FI-nisht'.

independentPractice.prompt: Budi wants to say 'Saya mau pergi sekarang', but he says 'I want to live now.' Which word should he say instead of 'live'?
independentPractice.hint: pergi = the word with the long 'ii'.

independentPractice.prompt: Which ending moves the stress to the syllable before it: -ful or -ic? Write it.
independentPractice.hint: Think of e-CON-o-my → e-co-NOM-ic and HELP → HELP-ful.

assessment.prompt: Budi tells a colleague: 'Yesterday I as my manager for a day off.' He dropped the last sounds of one word. Write the word he meant.
assessment.rubric: Correct: asked ('askt': s + k + t; 'yesterday' needs the past). 'ask' = 50 (right word, but the past ending t is still missing). 'as' or any other word = 0.

assessment.prompt: Listen. Do you hear text or texts? Write the word you hear.
assessment.rubric: Correct: texts (the final s after 'tekst' is clearly there: 'teksts'). text = 0 (the plural s was missed). A spelling slip like 'texs' = 50.

assessment.prompt: Listen. Do you hear live or leave? Write the word you hear.
assessment.rubric: Correct: live (a short, quick 'i': 'liv'). leave = 0 (that has a long 'ii': 'liiv').

assessment.prompt: Listen. Do you hear fan or van? Write the word you hear.
assessment.rubric: Correct: van (v = top teeth on the lower lip with a buzz). fan = 0 (f has no buzz). A spelling slip like 'vann' = 80.

assessment.prompt: After a meeting, Pak Hasan says: 'Tank you for your help.' Which word did he mean instead of 'tank'? Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: thank (th = tongue tip between the teeth; without it, thank becomes tank, tangki). 'thanks' = 80 (right sound, but the sentence needs thank). 'sank' or any other word = 0.

assessment.prompt: 'music' is stressed on the first syllable: MU-sic. Which syllable is stressed in 'musician' (mu-si-cian): first, second or third?
assessment.rubric: Correct: second (mu-SI-cian: -ian pulls the stress to the syllable just before it). first = 0 (that keeps the stress of music). third = 0.

assessment.prompt: Which syllable is stressed in 'scientific' (sci-en-ti-fic): first, second, third or fourth?
assessment.rubric: Correct: third (sci-en-TI-fic: -ic pulls the stress to the syllable just before it). first, second or fourth = 0.

material.title: Two or three consonants at the end

blocks.text:
A **consonant cluster** is two or three consonant sounds together, with no vowel between them. (A **consonant** is a 'huruf mati' sound like k, s, t, p, l.) You met easy ones in A1: *desk*, *lunch*. At B1 they get longer, because **grammar endings add more consonants**: -ed for the past, and -s for more than one or after he / she.
- *ask* + -ed = **asked** → 'askt' (s + k + t). British English says 'aaskt', American English 'askt'.
- *help* + -ed = **helped** → 'helpt' (l + p + t)
- *month* + -s = **months** → 'manths' (n + th + s)
- *text* + -s = **texts** → 'teksts' (k + s + t + s!)
- *crisp* + -s = **crisps** → 'krisps' (British *crisps* = American *chips* = keripik kentang)
- **next** → 'nekst'

**The Indonesian trap:** Indonesian words almost never end in two or three consonants. When Indonesian borrowed *text*, it became *teks*: the last t fell off! So learners say 'as' or 'ask' for *asked*, 'mon' for *months*, 'teks' for *texts*. The problem: **the ending carries the meaning**. Without the t, *I asked* becomes *I ask* (now, not the past); without the last s, *texts* becomes one *text*. The other mistake is adding a vowel: 'as-ked', 'help-e'.

id.text:
**Gugus konsonan** (consonant cluster) adalah dua atau tiga bunyi konsonan yang berdempetan, tanpa vokal di antaranya. (**Konsonan** = bunyi 'huruf mati' seperti k, s, t, p, l.) Kamu sudah bertemu yang mudah di A1: *desk*, *lunch*. Di B1 gugusnya lebih panjang, karena **akhiran tata bahasa menambah konsonan**: -ed untuk lampau, dan -s untuk lebih dari satu atau setelah he / she.
- *ask* + -ed = **asked** → 'askt' (s + k + t). Bahasa Inggris British mengucapkan 'aaskt', Amerika 'askt'.
- *help* + -ed = **helped** → 'helpt' (l + p + t)
- *month* + -s = **months** → 'manths' (n + th + s)
- *text* + -s = **texts** → 'teksts' (k + s + t + s!)
- *crisp* + -s = **crisps** → 'krisps' (*crisps* British = *chips* Amerika = keripik kentang)
- **next** → 'nekst'

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** kata bahasa Indonesia hampir tidak pernah berakhir dengan dua atau tiga konsonan. Waktu bahasa Indonesia meminjam kata *text*, jadinya *teks*: t terakhirnya hilang! Jadi pelajar mengucapkan 'as' atau 'ask' untuk *asked*, 'mon' untuk *months*, 'teks' untuk *texts*. Masalahnya: **akhiran itulah yang membawa makna**. Tanpa t, *I asked* jadi *I ask* (sekarang, bukan lampau); tanpa s terakhir, *texts* jadi satu *text* saja. Kesalahan lainnya adalah menambah vokal: 'as-ked', 'help-e'.

rows.note: 'manths': tongue between the teeth for th, then s

id.note: 'manths': lidah di antara gigi untuk th, lalu s

blocks.text:
**Slow, then fast.** Build a hard ending piece by piece, then speed up:
- 'as' → 'ask' → 'askt' → *I asked* → *I asked my boss.*
- 'man' → 'manth' → 'manths' → *six months*
Then look at the next word. Before a vowel, carry the last sound over: *asked a question* → 'ask-tə question', *six months ago* → 'manth-sə-GOU'. Before a consonant, keep it small and quick, with no extra vowel.

**A secret:** in fast speech, native speakers simplify the hardest endings too: *months* often sounds like 'mants', *texts* like 'tekss'. And *sixths* (1/6, 'siksths') is hard for everyone! You can simplify the middle, but **never drop the final s or t**: that's where the meaning is.

id.text:
**Pelan dulu, lalu cepat.** Bangun akhiran yang sulit sepotong demi sepotong, lalu percepat:
- 'as' → 'ask' → 'askt' → *I asked* → *I asked my boss.*
- 'man' → 'manth' → 'manths' → *six months*
Lalu lihat kata berikutnya. Sebelum vokal, sambungkan bunyi terakhir ke kata itu: *asked a question* → 'ask-tə question', *six months ago* → 'manth-sə-GOU'. Sebelum konsonan, ucapkan kecil dan cepat, tanpa vokal tambahan.

**Rahasia kecil:** dalam ucapan cepat, penutur asli juga menyederhanakan akhiran yang paling sulit: *months* sering terdengar seperti 'mants', *texts* seperti 'tekss'. Dan *sixths* (1/6, 'siksths') sulit untuk semua orang! Bagian tengahnya boleh kamu sederhanakan, tapi **jangan pernah menghilangkan s atau t terakhir**: di situlah maknanya.

blocks.prompt: Rina says: 'I lived in Bali for two mon.' Which word did she want to say?
blocks.explain: After *two* you need more than one: **months**, 'manths'. Rina dropped the th and the s, so the listener can't hear 'more than one'. Slow, then fast: 'man… manth… manths'.

id.prompt: Rina berkata: 'I lived in Bali for two mon.' Kata apa yang ingin dia ucapkan?
id.explain: Setelah *two* kamu butuh bentuk lebih dari satu: **months**, 'manths'. Rina menghilangkan th dan s, jadi pendengar tidak bisa menangkap 'lebih dari satu'. Pelan dulu, lalu cepat: 'man… manth… manths'.

id.title: Dua atau tiga konsonan di akhir kata

material.title: Short or long: live / leave, full / fool

blocks.text:
A **minimal pair** is two words that differ in **only one sound**, like Indonesian *pagi / bagi* or *tari / dari*. Many English minimal pairs differ only in a **short or long vowel**, and Indonesian has just one i and one u, so they easily sound the same. In A0 you met *ship / sheep*. Now use them in real sentences, where the wrong sound changes the message:
- **short 'i'**: quick and relaxed: *live* 'liv', *fill* 'fil', *sit* 'sit'
- **long 'ii'**: held longer, lips spread like a smile: *leave* 'liiv', *feel* 'fiil', *seat* 'siit'
- **short 'u'**: quick, lips relaxed: *full* 'ful', *pull* 'pul'
- **long 'uu'**: held longer, lips round and pushed forward: *fool* 'fuul', *pool* 'puul'

Why it matters: *I want to leave* (pergi) said with a short i becomes *I want to live* (hidup / tinggal). *The bus is full* (penuh) said with a long 'uu' sounds like *fool* (orang bodoh)!

**Spelling clues:** *ee* and *ea* are usually the long 'ii' (*feel, leave, seat*). With *oo* you can't be sure: long in *fool, pool, food*, short in *good, book*. Learn each word with its sound.

id.text:
**Minimal pair** adalah dua kata yang **hanya beda satu bunyi**, seperti *pagi / bagi* atau *tari / dari* dalam bahasa Indonesia. Banyak minimal pair bahasa Inggris hanya beda di **vokal pendek atau panjang**, dan bahasa Indonesia hanya punya satu i dan satu u, jadi keduanya gampang terdengar sama. Di A0 kamu sudah bertemu *ship / sheep*. Sekarang pakai di kalimat nyata, di mana bunyi yang salah mengubah pesannya:
- **'i' pendek**: cepat dan santai: *live* 'liv', *fill* 'fil', *sit* 'sit'
- **'ii' panjang**: ditahan lebih lama, bibir melebar seperti tersenyum: *leave* 'liiv', *feel* 'fiil', *seat* 'siit'
- **'u' pendek**: cepat, bibir santai: *full* 'ful', *pull* 'pul'
- **'uu' panjang**: ditahan lebih lama, bibir bulat dan maju: *fool* 'fuul', *pool* 'puul'

Kenapa penting: *I want to leave* (pergi) yang diucapkan dengan i pendek jadi *I want to live* (hidup / tinggal). *The bus is full* (penuh) yang diucapkan dengan 'uu' panjang terdengar seperti *fool* (orang bodoh)!

**Petunjuk ejaan:** *ee* dan *ea* biasanya 'ii' panjang (*feel, leave, seat*). Untuk *oo* kamu tidak bisa yakin: panjang di *fool, pool, food*, pendek di *good, book*. Pelajari setiap kata bersama bunyinya.

rows.note: leave = 'liiv': a long 'ii', and a v at the end (not 'liif')

id.note: leave = 'liiv': 'ii' panjang, dan v di akhir (bukan 'liif')

rows.note: fool = 'fuul', a long 'uu' with round lips

blocks.text: **Feel the length.** Say a pair slowly: hold the long sound for two counts and the short one for one: 'liv' (1), 'lii-iv' (1-2). Then say them fast inside a sentence. Record yourself on your phone: if *live* and *leave* sound the same, smile more and hold the long one longer.

id.text: **Rasakan panjangnya.** Ucapkan pasangannya pelan-pelan: tahan bunyi panjang selama dua hitungan dan bunyi pendek satu hitungan: 'liv' (1), 'lii-iv' (1-2). Lalu ucapkan dengan cepat di dalam kalimat. Rekam suaramu di HP: kalau *live* dan *leave* terdengar sama, tersenyumlah lebih lebar dan tahan bunyi panjangnya lebih lama.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence has a long 'ii' sound?
blocks.explain: *leave* has the long 'ii' ('liiv', ea = long 'ii'). *live* ('liv') and *fill* ('fil') have the short, quick i.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang punya bunyi 'ii' panjang?
id.explain: *leave* punya 'ii' panjang ('liiv', ea = 'ii' panjang). *live* ('liv') dan *fill* ('fil') punya i pendek yang cepat.

id.title: Pendek atau panjang: live / leave, full / fool

material.title: f or v, s or th: fan / van, sink / think

blocks.text:
Some consonant pairs are hard because Indonesian doesn't really use one of the two sounds.

**f or v?** For both, your **top teeth touch your lower lip**. For **f** only air comes out. For **v** your **voice buzzes** too: put your hand on your throat and you feel it shake. In Indonesian the letter v is usually said like f (*visa, televisi*), so English *van* easily becomes *fan*:
- *fan* (kipas angin / penggemar) – *van* (mobil van)
- *ferry* (kapal feri) – *very* (sangat)
- *safe* (aman) – *save* (menyimpan / menabung)

**th, s or t?** For the th of *think*, put the **tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth** and push air out. If your tongue stays behind your teeth, you get **s** or **t**:
- *think* (berpikir) – *sink* (wastafel / tenggelam)
- *thank* (berterima kasih) – *tank* (tangki)
- *three* (tiga) – *tree* (pohon)

id.text:
Beberapa pasangan konsonan sulit karena bahasa Indonesia tidak benar-benar memakai salah satu bunyinya.

**f atau v?** Untuk keduanya, **gigi atas menyentuh bibir bawah**. Untuk **f** hanya udara yang keluar. Untuk **v** **suaramu ikut bergetar**: taruh tangan di tenggorokan dan kamu akan merasakan getarannya. Dalam bahasa Indonesia, huruf v biasanya dibaca seperti f (*visa, televisi*), jadi *van* gampang terucap *fan*:
- *fan* (kipas angin / penggemar) – *van* (mobil van)
- *ferry* (kapal feri) – *very* (sangat)
- *safe* (aman) – *save* (menyimpan / menabung)

**th, s atau t?** Untuk th di *think*, taruh **ujung lidah dengan ringan di antara gigi** lalu hembuskan udara. Kalau lidahmu tetap di belakang gigi, yang keluar jadi **s** atau **t**:
- *think* (berpikir) – *sink* (wastafel / tenggelam)
- *thank* (berterima kasih) – *tank* (tangki)
- *three* (tiga) – *tree* (pohon)

rows.en: Pak Hasan drives a white van.
rows.id: Pak Hasan menyetir mobil van putih.
rows.note: van: teeth on the lip + a buzz

rows.en: It's hot. Turn on the fan.
Save your work before you close the file.
rows.note: save ends in v: keep the buzz

id.note: save berakhiran v: getarnya tetap ada

rows.en: I think the meeting is at ten.
rows.note: think: tongue between the teeth, not 'sink' or 'tink'

id.note: think: lidah di antara gigi, bukan 'sink' atau 'tink'

rows.en: There are three trees in the garden.

blocks.text: **Mirror and throat test.** For th, you should see the tip of your tongue in a mirror. For v, put your hand on your throat: *ffff* is quiet, *vvvv* buzzes. Slow, then fast: 'fff… fan', 'vvv… van', then *a fan and a van*.

id.text: **Tes cermin dan tenggorokan.** Untuk th, ujung lidahmu harus kelihatan di cermin. Untuk v, taruh tangan di tenggorokan: *ffff* diam, *vvvv* bergetar. Pelan dulu, lalu cepat: 'fff… fan', 'vvv… van', lalu *a fan and a van*.

blocks.prompt: Rina says: 'The film was fery good.' What should she change?
options: Top teeth on the lower lip, with a buzz: very
blocks.explain: She means **very** (sangat). v and f are made in the same place (top teeth on the lower lip), but v **buzzes**. Without the buzz, *very* sounds like *ferry* (kapal feri).

id.prompt: Rina berkata: 'The film was fery good.' Apa yang harus dia ubah?
id.explain: Maksudnya **very** (sangat). v dan f dibuat di tempat yang sama (gigi atas di bibir bawah), tapi v **bergetar**. Tanpa getar, *very* terdengar seperti *ferry* (kapal feri).

id.title: f atau v, s atau th: fan / van, sink / think

blocks.text:
In the word formation lesson you built families like *decide / decision / decisive*. When you say a family out loud, watch one more thing: the **stress** (the strong syllable: louder, longer, a little higher, written here in CAPITALS) can **move** when you add an ending.
- **PHO**-to-graph → pho-**TO**-gra-phy → pho-to-**GRA**-phic
- **PO**-li-tics → po-**LI**-ti-cal → po-li-**TI**-cian
- e-**CON**-o-my → e-co-**NOM**-ic (careful: *economy* is not stressed on the first syllable)
- **ED**-u-cate → ed-u-**CA**-tion
- **AC**-tive → ac-**TI**-vi-ty

**The helpful rule:** these endings pull the stress to the syllable **just before** them: **-ic, -ical, -ian, -tion / -sion, -ity, -graphy**.
These endings **don't** move it: **-er, -ment, -ful, -less, -ly**: **TEACH**-er, em-**PLOY**-ment, **HELP**-ful, **CARE**-less.
**An exception to remember:** *photographer* follows *photography*, not the -er rule: pho-**TO**-gra-pher. (And you know em-ploy-**EE** from the word formation lesson: -ee takes the stress itself.)

**The vowels change too.** Only the strong syllable has a clear vowel; the others often become the lazy schwa ə (the short e of *emas*): *photograph* 'FOU-tə-graaf' (American 'FOU-tə-graf'), *photography* 'fə-TOG-rə-fi'.

**The Indonesian trap:** we have similar words (*fotografi, ekonomi, politik*) and say them with an even rhythm, so learners keep one stress for the whole family: 'pho-TO-graph', 'PHO-to-gra-phy'. English listeners recognise a word by its stress, so the wrong one can make a word you know well hard to understand.

id.text:
Di pelajaran pembentukan kata kamu sudah membangun keluarga kata seperti *decide / decision / decisive*. Saat kamu mengucapkan satu keluarga kata, perhatikan satu hal lagi: **tekanan** (suku kata yang kuat: lebih keras, lebih panjang, sedikit lebih tinggi, di sini ditulis HURUF BESAR) bisa **berpindah** saat kamu menambah akhiran.
- **PHO**-to-graph → pho-**TO**-gra-phy → pho-to-**GRA**-phic
- **PO**-li-tics → po-**LI**-ti-cal → po-li-**TI**-cian
- e-**CON**-o-my → e-co-**NOM**-ic (hati-hati: *economy* tidak ditekan di suku kata pertama)
- **ED**-u-cate → ed-u-**CA**-tion
- **AC**-tive → ac-**TI**-vi-ty

**Aturan yang membantu:** akhiran-akhiran ini menarik tekanan ke suku kata **tepat sebelum** akhiran itu: **-ic, -ical, -ian, -tion / -sion, -ity, -graphy**.
Akhiran-akhiran ini **tidak** memindahkannya: **-er, -ment, -ful, -less, -ly**: **TEACH**-er, em-**PLOY**-ment, **HELP**-ful, **CARE**-less.
**Pengecualian yang perlu diingat:** *photographer* mengikuti *photography*, bukan aturan -er: pho-**TO**-gra-pher. (Dan kamu sudah tahu em-ploy-**EE** dari pelajaran pembentukan kata: -ee mengambil tekanannya sendiri.)

**Vokalnya juga berubah.** Hanya suku kata yang kuat yang vokalnya jelas; yang lain sering jadi schwa ə yang malas (e pendek seperti di *emas*): *photograph* 'FOU-tə-graaf' (Amerika 'FOU-tə-graf'), *photography* 'fə-TOG-rə-fi'.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** kita punya kata yang mirip (*fotografi, ekonomi, politik*) dan mengucapkannya dengan irama yang rata, jadi pelajar memakai satu tekanan untuk seluruh keluarga kata: 'pho-TO-graph', 'PHO-to-gra-phy'. Pendengar bahasa Inggris mengenali kata dari tekanannya, jadi tekanan yang salah bisa membuat kata yang sebenarnya kamu kuasai jadi sulit dipahami.

rows.note: pho-TO-gra-pher: like photography, not like TEACH-er

id.note: pho-TO-gra-pher: seperti photography, bukan seperti TEACH-er

blocks.text: **Check it once, say it right forever.** When you learn a new long word, check its stress in a dictionary (the high mark ˈ comes just before the strong syllable, as you learnt in A1) and press the speaker button. Then say the whole family out loud and clap loudly on the strong syllable: CLAP-clap-clap (PHO-to-graph), clap-CLAP-clap-clap (pho-TO-gra-phy).

id.text: **Cek sekali, ucapkan benar selamanya.** Saat mempelajari kata panjang yang baru, cek tekanannya di kamus (tanda tinggi ˈ ada tepat sebelum suku kata yang kuat, seperti yang kamu pelajari di A1) lalu tekan tombol speaker. Kemudian ucapkan seluruh keluarga katanya dengan suara keras, dan tepuk keras di suku kata yang kuat: PROK-prok-prok (PHO-to-graph), prok-PROK-prok-prok (pho-TO-gra-phy).

blocks.prompt: Which word is stressed on the second syllable?
blocks.explain: **political** = po-LI-ti-cal: -ical pulls the stress to the syllable just before it, the second one. *photograph* is PHO-to-graph (first) and *politician* is po-li-TI-cian (third, just before -ian).

id.prompt: Kata mana yang ditekan di suku kata kedua?
id.explain: **political** = po-LI-ti-cal: -ical menarik tekanan ke suku kata tepat sebelumnya, yaitu yang kedua. *photograph* = PHO-to-graph (pertama) dan *politician* = po-li-TI-cian (ketiga, tepat sebelum -ian).

suggestedQuestions: Do native speakers really say every sound in 'texts'?
How can I hear the difference between live and leave?
Why does the stress move in photography but not in employment?
How do I make a v if my mouth keeps saying f?

resources.title: Consonant Clusters (Pronouncing sixth, twelfth, texts, crisps ...)
resources.note: An 8-minute British English lesson on hard endings like texts and crisps, with a step-by-step way to build them up. It also shows sixths and twelfths, which are hard even for natives. The video mentions the channel's paid course: you don't need it.

id.note: Pelajaran 8 menit dalam bahasa Inggris British tentang akhiran sulit seperti texts dan crisps, dengan cara membangunnya selangkah demi selangkah. Video ini juga menunjukkan sixths dan twelfths, yang sulit bahkan untuk penutur asli. Videonya menyebut kursus berbayar dari channel itu: kamu tidak membutuhkannya.

resources.title: Ship or sheep? The English long vowel /iː/ and short vowel /ɪ/
resources.note: A one-minute BBC short on the long 'ii' of sheep and the short 'i' of ship. The same difference as live / leave and fill / feel: listen and repeat.

id.note: Video pendek satu menit dari BBC tentang 'ii' panjang di sheep dan 'i' pendek di ship. Bedanya sama dengan live / leave dan fill / feel: dengarkan dan tirukan.

resources.title: How Word Stress Changes in English | Root Words & Word Families – Part 1
resources.note: A 5-minute American English lesson on how stress moves in word families, including photo / photograph / photography / photographic. Some example words (residency, collaborative) are above B1: focus on how the strong syllable moves.

id.note: Pelajaran 5 menit dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika tentang bagaimana tekanan berpindah dalam keluarga kata, termasuk photo / photograph / photography / photographic. Beberapa contoh katanya (residency, collaborative) di atas level B1: fokus saja pada bagaimana suku kata yang kuat berpindah.

flashcards.back: 'askt': s + k + t, one beat (not 'as' or 'ask')

flashcards.front: months / texts: apa yang tidak boleh hilang?

flashcards.back: top teeth on the lower lip + a buzz; not f
tongue tip between the teeth, air only; not s or t
stress just before the ending: pho-TO-gra-phy, po-li-TI-cian, e-co-NOM-ic
the stress doesn't move: TEACH-er, em-PLOY-ment (but pho-TO-gra-pher)

id.intro: Hari ini kamu memoles tiga hal yang membuat bahasa Inggrismu mudah dipahami: akhiran dengan dua atau tiga konsonan (asked = 'askt', months, texts), pasangan kata yang hanya beda satu bunyi (live / leave, fan / van), dan tekanan yang berpindah di dalam satu keluarga kata (PHO-to-graph → pho-TO-gra-phy). Pemanasan: ucapkan 'I asked for six months' pelan-pelan, lalu cepat.
suggestedQuestions: Apakah penutur asli benar-benar mengucapkan semua bunyi di 'texts'?
Bagaimana cara mendengar beda live dan leave?
Kenapa tekanan berpindah di photography tapi tidak di employment?
Bagaimana cara mengucapkan v kalau mulutku terus mengucapkan f?

assessment.ccp-1: Budi berkata kepada rekan kerjanya: 'Yesterday I as my manager for a day off.' Dia menghilangkan bunyi terakhir dari satu kata. Tulis kata yang dia maksud (dalam bahasa Inggris).
assessment.ccp-2: Dengarkan. Kamu mendengar text atau texts? Tulis kata yang kamu dengar.
assessment.ccp-3: Dengarkan. Kamu mendengar live atau leave? Tulis kata yang kamu dengar.
assessment.ccp-4: Dengarkan. Kamu mendengar fan atau van? Tulis kata yang kamu dengar.
assessment.ccp-5: Setelah rapat, Pak Hasan berkata: 'Tank you for your help.' Kata apa yang dia maksud, sebagai ganti 'tank'? Tulis kata itu (dalam bahasa Inggris).
assessment.ccp-6: 'music' ditekan di suku kata pertama: MU-sic. Suku kata mana yang ditekan di 'musician' (mu-si-cian): first, second atau third? Tulis jawabannya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ccp-7: Suku kata mana yang ditekan di 'scientific' (sci-en-ti-fic): first, second, third atau fourth? Tulis jawabannya dalam bahasa Inggris.
